```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", message = FALSE)
```

gratia supports scam's univariate and bivariate shape-constrained smooth
constructors, including cyclic margins, endpoint constraints, local constraints,
`by` smooths and smooth interactions. This includes the `tedi` and `teid` tensor
constructors introduced in scam 1.2-23, which constrain one covariate's effect
to increase and the other's to decrease. These two constructors require a
scam version that provides them. Ordinary mgcv smooths fitted through
`scam()` are also supported. The same fitted coefficient mapping is used for
smooth estimates, bases, derivatives, predictions and sampled smooths.

We load gratia and scam before simulating the example.
```{r packages}
library("gratia")
load_mgcv()
library("scam")
```

The response below combines an increasing curved effect of `x` and a linear
effect of `z`, with independent Gaussian noise of standard deviation 0.15.
The covariates are independently sampled on the unit interval.
```{r simulate-data}
set.seed(46)
d <- data.frame(x = runif(200), z = runif(200))
d$y <- exp(d$x) + d$z + rnorm(nrow(d), sd = 0.15)
```

We fit increasing smooths for both covariates and plot their estimated contributions.
```{r fit-model}
m <- scam(y ~ s(x, bs = "mpi", k = 8) + s(z, bs = "mpi", k = 8),
  data = d, not.exp = TRUE)
draw(m)
```

## Fitted functions and native plots

Plot captions describe basis and shape separately. Increasing and decreasing
constraints use arrows; tensor captions name the covariate for each constraint.
Local constraints show their fitted change point. These captions are also
available when drawing saved `smooth_estimates()`. The `.type` column and
`smooth_type()` retain compact ASCII labels such as `P spline (inc)` and
`Tensor (inc, free)`.

By default, `draw()` retains the fitted function's centring. Evaluating a
smooth on a different grid therefore evaluates the same function. This agrees
with scam's univariate plots. Its bivariate plots instead subtract the mean
of the evaluated surface. Use `centre = "plot"` to match that convention;
both estimates and their covariance receive the same centring operation.
`assemble()` accepts the same argument. Match grids and exclusion distances
when comparing plots from the two packages.

```{r surface}
b <- scam(y ~ s(x, z, bs = "tedmi", k = c(5, 5)), data = d,
  not.exp = TRUE)
draw(b, centre = "plot", n_2d = 40)
```

scam's default univariate limits use two standard errors; gratia's default
95% normal limits use `qnorm(0.975)`. Some scam smooth classes also use a
different coefficient gradient for the displayed function and its standard
error. gratia computes uncertainty for the actual function it returns, using
its coefficient gradient. This can produce different limits even when the
fitted curves agree.

## Conditional uncertainty and sampled functions

Pointwise intervals, simultaneous smooth bands, smooth derivatives and contrasts use
scam's covariance for the transformed coefficients (`Vp.t`, or `Ve.t` with
`frequentist = TRUE`). These are local Gaussian or delta approximations,
conditional on the fitted smoothing parameters. Including intercept
uncertainty is controlled by `overall_uncertainty`.

```{r estimates}
e <- smooth_estimates(m, overall_uncertainty = FALSE)
e <- add_confint(e)
head(e)
derivatives(m, select = "s(x)")
confint(m, parm = "s(x)", type = "simultaneous", seed = 53)
```

Coefficient sampling uses a different approximation: draw a Gaussian vector in
the unrestricted fitting coordinates using `Vp` (or `Ve`), then apply the
positivity transformation used in the fit. This preserves the fitted shape
constraints. This is a Gaussian approximation in fitting coordinates, rather
than an exact constrained posterior. Because the transformation is nonlinear,
these samples need not have the mean or covariance used for analytic intervals. Individual analytic
interval endpoints need not satisfy the shape constraint.

Fitted, smooth, derivative and response sampling functions project these same
transformed coefficient draws. `response_derivatives()` also uses them with its
default `uncertainty = "simulation"`; `uncertainty = "delta"` instead uses the
local transformed-coefficient covariance.

```{r samples}
draws <- gaussian_draws(m, n_draws = 100, seed = 54)
samples <- smooth_samples(m, n_draws = 5, seed = 55)
head(samples)
```

`method = "user"` requires finite draws in the transformed coordinates, with
columns in `coef(m)` order and nonnegative constrained coefficients.
`gaussian_draws(m, parametrized = FALSE)` returns unrestricted draws for
inspection; these cannot be supplied as transformed draws. A singular
positive semidefinite covariance is supported. A materially indefinite
covariance is rejected. When a very large unrestricted variance causes the
exponential transformation to overflow, sampling reports an error; it does
not truncate those draws. Finite transformed draws from an appropriate
alternative sampler can still be supplied.

## Predictions and model checks

To predict the mean response as `x` varies, use `conditional_values()`. It
combines both smooths and the intercept, holding `z` at its median in the
fitting data. The bands show uncertainty in the mean response.

```{r conditional-predictions}
predictions <- conditional_values(m, condition = "x")
predictions
draw(predictions)
```

Use `appraise()` to check the fitted response distribution and look for
remaining patterns in the residuals. Here, quantile residuals compare each
observation with its fitted Gaussian distribution. Inspect the QQ plot for
departures from its reference line and the residual-versus-predictor panel
for curvature or changes in spread.

```{r model-checks}
appraise(m, type = "quantile", seed = 56)
```

The [model diagnostics article](model-checking.html) explains how to interpret
these panels and their reference bands.
